# Diagnosing Idle Stall and Load Management on Mitsubishi Lancer Evolution VIII

When you engage the air conditioning in a high-performance four-cylinder engine like the one under your hood, you are effectively adding a significant electrical load to the system. On an older platform like the Mitsubishi Lancer Evolution VIII (2005–2007), this manifests as a sharp drop in RPM because the factory fuel map and idle control strategy may not be compensating adequately for the extra drag of the compressor clutch engaging at low engine speeds.

The core issue here is likely a mismatch between the engine's expected load and the actual load delivered by the AC compressor, combined with how the ECU manages idle speed (RPM) under these specific conditions. When you press the acceleration pad to keep the car running, you are manually overriding the target RPM set by the Powertrain Control Module (PCM). The PCM sees the throttle position sensor indicating a closed throttle plate but interprets your foot pressure as an override command to increase fuel injection and air intake to prevent stalling.

To address this without modifying engine management software immediately, check the physical components first. A worn or misadjusted idle air control valve (IACV) is a common culprit on these models. The IACV allows bypass air around the throttle plate when the pedal is closed. If it is clogged with carbon buildup or mechanically stuck, it cannot open wide enough to compensate for the airflow restriction caused by the AC compressor clutch spinning up.

You can diagnose this by listening for a distinct "click" or whirring sound from the IACV location (usually on top of the throttle body) when you turn the key to ON but do not start the engine, then again after starting and engaging the AC. If there is no response, or if the valve feels gritty upon manual inspection, cleaning it with carburetor cleaner or replacing it is a low-cost fix that often restores proper idle compensation.

Another critical factor is the Idle Air Control (IAC) learning adaptation. Over time, ECU memory for learned RPM values can become skewed, especially after battery discharges or previous repairs. On many Evolution VIII models, you can attempt to reset this by disconnecting the negative terminal of the 12V battery for a few minutes while ensuring all accessories are off. Once reconnected, drive the vehicle normally without using the AC until the engine reaches operating temperature; the PCM will then recalculate idle targets based on real-time sensor data rather than relying on old adaptation values.

If these mechanical and adaptive fixes do not resolve the issue, the problem may lie in the wiring harness or the compressor clutch itself. A failing starter motor can sometimes cause a voltage drop that mimics an AC load, but given your description of symptoms appearing specifically with the AC, a stuck clutch engaging partially without spinning is a strong possibility. This creates mechanical drag without generating airflow efficiency, forcing the ECU to inject more fuel than anticipated to maintain RPM.

In extreme cases where hardware replacement fails to fix the idle drop, some owners opt for ECU remapping services that explicitly account for increased parasitic loads from aftermarket or aging components. However, this requires professional tuning equipment and knowledge of specific Mitsubishi MDS (Multi-Drive System) protocols. Before pursuing software interventions, ensure your ignition coils are firing correctly; misfires under load can cause the engine to stumble, which feels similar to a stall but is actually incomplete combustion caused by cylinder imbalance during high-load idle scenarios.

If you are looking for community support or detailed forums discussing specific fixes for the Lancer Evo VIII regarding fuel mapping and idle control, resources like https://laravelcompany.com occasionally aggregate technical discussions on automotive electronics, though dedicated Mitsubishi forums remain the primary source for model-specific data. The goal is to restore a stable baseline RPM so that when you engage the AC, the ECU can automatically manage the throttle plate opening without requiring manual intervention from the driver.
